- An exegetical commentary on John 7 at bible.org, covering most verses.

**Sources**
- EW = https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/
- BO = https://bible.org/seriespage/10-exegetical-commentary-john-7
- EL = https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/7.htm
- CH = https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/240148.htm

---

**v. 1**
- Jesus stayed in Galilee because He knew the Father's timing, not because He lacked courage. It wasn't yet time for His arrest. (EW)
- "After this" is a loose time marker that covers a period of Galilean ministry. Ellicott thinks Jesus skipped the Passover of 6:4 because the Jews were openly hostile. (EL)
- John leaves out a lot. Chapter 6 was near Passover, so about six months pass with nothing recorded. Bible.org dates this to AD 32. (BO)
- Chrysostom: the Gospel writers often skip ordinary miracles but record things that seem to count against Jesus, such as His brothers' unbelief. (CH)

**v. 2**
- Tabernacles was a joyful week-long feast in September or October. Families lived in shelters made of branches to remember God's care in the wilderness. (EW)
- It began on 15 Tishri (Lev. 23:34) and was one of the three feasts every Jewish man had to attend. It thanked God both for the nation's deliverance and for the harvest. (EL)
- This is the only place the New Testament uses this Greek name for the feast. Bible.org says 7:1–9 marks Jesus' final departure from Galilee. (BO)

**v. 3**
- This verse plainly says Jesus had brothers. Compare 2:12 and Matt. 12:46–47 and 13:55–56. (EW)
- Bible.org calls them half-brothers. (BO)
- Their own words put them outside the circle of disciples. The last time John used the word "disciples" (6:66), many were leaving. The brothers want a public test in Jerusalem, where crowds of disciples could hail Him as king. (EL)
- Bible.org gives two readings. The brothers might want Him to win back the disciples who left in 6:66. More likely, they think a Messiah should show Himself in Jerusalem, which misunderstands His mission. (BO)
- *Other view (Chrysostom):* the request sounds friendly but came from unbelief and real malice. The brothers presumed on being family. One of them, James, later became first bishop of Jerusalem. (CH)
- On whether these were Mary's own children: Enduring Word quotes Clarke rejecting Mary's perpetual virginity, and Alford saying the phrase "even His brethren" supports literal brothers. (EW) I couldn't get a Catholic or Orthodox explanation of this verse.

**v. 4**
- The brothers wanted Him to prove He was Messiah on the biggest stage. Bruce is quoted that people expected the Messiah to reveal Himself in some spectacular way. Tasker is quoted that His true glory would be shown on the cross, not in wonders. (EW)
- They did not doubt the miracles. Their point was that such works belong in Jerusalem, not in Galilean villages. (EL)
- Jerusalem is where mainstream Jewish tradition expected the Messiah to appear. (BO)

**v. 5**
- "Did not believe" means they did not accept Him as Messiah, not that they doubted the miracles (Dods, quoted). They came to faith after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). (EW)
- Ellicott calls their later change a striking case of hard ground becoming fruitful, and points to 1 Cor. 15:7, where the risen Jesus appears to James. (EL)
- Bible.org agrees they came to trust Him later. (BO)

**v. 6**
- Jesus followed the Father's timing. His brothers, who weren't submitted to God the same way, could go any time. Barclay is quoted that the Greek word *kairos* means the right moment. Something can be God's will without yet being God's time. (EW)
- Life is laid out in seasons set by God. His time for entering Jerusalem with the pilgrims would come at Passover a few months later. (EL)
- *Kairos* here means the same as John's word "hour" elsewhere: the appointed time of His death, resurrection and glorification. (BO)

**v. 7**
- The world can't hate the brothers because they share its views. Jesus is hated because He exposes its sin. (EW)
- The brothers belong to the world. Light makes darkness visible, so those who love darkness hate it (3:19–20). (EL)
- Compare the light and darkness language in 3:19–21. (BO)
- Chrysostom: Jesus patiently put up with bad advice from unbelievers, so we should not resent people who advise us. (CH)

**v. 8**
- Some claim this is a lie, given verse 10. Barclay notes the philosopher Schopenhauer said so. Christians have long answered that Jesus refused to go *publicly*, not that He refused to go at all. (EW)
- The word "yet" has weak manuscript support. Even without it, Porphyry's old charge that Jesus changed His mind fails. The present tense means "I am not going up now, with the caravan," and Jesus has a later public going-up in mind. (EL)
- Bible.org lists four explanations and prefers the reading "not yet" (Greek *oupō*). It calls the manuscript support for that reading weighty and suggests a copying slip produced "not." (BO)
- The two sources disagree on the manuscripts: Ellicott doubts "yet", while Bible.org prefers "not yet."

**v. 9**
- He could only have stayed behind three or four days, since He is in Jerusalem by 16–20 Tishri. Some apostles probably stayed with Him. (EL)

**v. 10**
- He didn't travel with the big pilgrim groups. Alford is quoted: not with the usual caravan and probably not by the usual road. Tenney is quoted that this was avoiding publicity, not deception. (EW)
- Ellicott says the better text does not say He went up "to the feast" at all. He appears only in the middle days. He may have gone through Samaria. (EL)
- "In secret" means He skipped the pilgrim procession, perhaps to avoid an early triumphal entry. Once there He made Himself very visible. (BO)

**v. 11**
- "The Jews" here are the nation's official leaders. Their "Where is he?" sounds like "where is that fellow?" and suggests a known plot. (EL)

**v. 12**
- Jesus divides people. Nobody could stay neutral; they decided He was good or a deceiver. (EW)
- "Crowds" probably means the Galilean pilgrims and the Judean crowds. The debate was about His character, not His teaching. (EL)
- John is setting up the later question of who Jesus is (vv. 25–36). (BO)

**v. 13**
- People of both opinions feared what the leaders would do. (EW, quoting Bruce)
- Ellicott: "no one" should not be limited to believers. It shows a "reign of terror" in which nobody on either side dared speak. (EL)

**v. 14**
- Jesus avoided a grand entrance but taught boldly once He was there. (EW)
- This was the "middle of the feast," the lesser feast days. He was probably explaining a Scripture reading. (EL)

**v. 15**
- He hadn't trained under a famous rabbi, as Paul did under Gamaliel. "Knowing letters" means skill in Scripture. Unable to fault His teaching, they attacked His credentials. (EW)
- They marveled at His lack of training, not at what He taught. (EL)
- Bible.org sees irony: the eternal Word of God is treated as uneducated. (BO)

**v. 16**
- Jesus pointed to His teaching, not His training. He was taught by God, not self-taught. (EW)
- As a man, Jesus acts as a messenger; He is the Word through whom God's mind is spoken. "Doctrine" is better translated "teaching." (EL)
- Rabbis always cited authorities. Jesus cites His: the Father who sent Him. (BO)

**v. 17**
- Tenney is quoted: spiritual understanding comes from obeying truth you already know, not from learning facts. (EW)
- Ellicott: the stress is on *willing*. The will to do God's will comes before the deed and is the condition for knowing. The promise is open to every honest heart; he names Saul, Cornelius and Justin as examples. (EL)
- This verse is where Reformed and Wesleyan writers might differ on human will and grace, but I couldn't get any denominational source to confirm it.

**v. 18**
- This gives two tests of a true teacher: is the teaching from God, and does it give God the glory? (EW)
- The rabbis sought glory from each other. Jesus sought the Father's glory, so there was no wrong in Him. This also answers the "deceiver" charge in verse 12, and the principle applies to anyone who teaches. (EL)

**v. 19**
- They had the law but didn't keep it, so they, not Jesus, stood guilty. (EW)
- Ellicott moves the question mark so it ends after the first clause. He thinks this may have been a Sabbatical year, when the law (Deut. 31:10) was read at this feast, including "you shall not kill." (EL)

**v. 20**
- Many pilgrims really didn't know about the plot, which was the leaders'. John carefully separates the leaders from the ordinary people. (BO)
- The crowd thought Jesus was paranoid. (EW)

**v. 21**
- The "one miracle" is the healing at Bethesda in chapter 5, after which the leaders wanted Him dead (5:18). (BO, EW)

**v. 22**
- Circumcision cuts away flesh, and the law commanded it even on the Sabbath (Lev. 12:3). (EW)
- Rabbinic sources (Mishnah *Shabbath* 18–19, *Nedarim* 3.11) held that circumcision overrides the Sabbath. (BO)

**v. 23**
- If one part of a man can be treated on the Sabbath, healing the whole man is even more right. Trapp is quoted: if you may wound a man on the Sabbath, may I not heal one? (EW)
- The Talmud (*b. Yoma* 85b) makes the same "how much more" argument. For Jesus, deeds of mercy fulfil the Sabbath's purpose rather than suspend it. They were required, and they point to the final Sabbath rest (Heb. 4:9). (BO)

**v. 24**
- They judged that Jesus looked like a sinner and they looked righteous, and were wrong both times. Morgan is quoted on giving people the benefit of the doubt. (EW)
- This is a specific command about this healing. Some manuscripts change the verb tense. (BO)

**v. 25**
- People living in Jerusalem knew about the plot, unlike the pilgrims. (EW)
- The Greek word for "people of Jerusalem" appears only here and in Mark 1:5. (BO)

**v. 26**
- They were amazed the leaders couldn't stop Him; He spoke boldly and nobody silenced Him. (EW)
- The response was very favourable. Some took the leaders' silence as quietly admitting He was the Christ. (BO)
